title: Can Arthritis Be Prevented?
meta_title: Can Arthritis Be Prevented? What You Can and Can't Change

content:
You cannot always prevent arthritis, because some risk factors such as age, genes and sex cannot be changed. But you can lower your risk of some types, especially osteoarthritis and gout, and reduce how much arthritis affects you if you do develop it. The most useful steps are keeping to a healthy weight, staying active, protecting your joints from injury and not smoking.

Risk factors you cannot change

  • age: osteoarthritis becomes more common over 45
  • sex: osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are more common in women, gout in men
  • genes and family history: some types run in families
  • past joint problems present from birth or childhood

Knowing these does not mean arthritis is certain. It means the changeable factors matter even more.

Keep to a healthy weight

Extra body weight increases the load on knees, hips and feet with every step. Fat tissue also releases chemicals that can promote inflammation. Being overweight is one of the biggest risk factors for knee osteoarthritis and is also linked with gout and more active inflammatory arthritis. Even modest weight loss reduces strain on joints. The NHS offers free weight-management support, including the NHS Weight Loss Plan app.

Stay active and strong

Regular activity keeps joints moving and muscles strong. Strong thigh muscles, for example, help protect the knee. The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, plus strength exercises on two days. Low-impact activities such as walking, swimming and cycling are easy on joints. If you play sport, a mix of activities reduces repeated strain on the same joints.

Protect your joints from injury

Joint injuries, such as a torn knee ligament or cartilage, raise the risk of osteoarthritis in that joint later in life. To reduce your risk:

  • warm up before sport and build up training gradually
  • learn good technique, particularly for twisting and landing movements
  • wear the right footwear and protective equipment
  • get a significant joint injury assessed and complete the rehabilitation exercises
  • at work, use lifting aids and follow manual handling advice

Do not smoke

Smoking is the strongest lifestyle risk factor for rheumatoid arthritis, and it also makes RA more severe. It affects bone health and healing too. Free NHS stop smoking services can help you quit.

Limit alcohol and sugary drinks

For gout, drinking a lot of alcohol, especially beer and spirits, and sugary drinks raise uric acid levels and the risk of attacks. Keeping within the UK low-risk guideline of 14 units a week spread over several days, and drinking plenty of water, helps.

Look after your bones and muscles as you age

Muscle strength and balance decline with age unless we use them. Strength and balance exercise reduces falls and fractures and keeps you mobile. Eat a balanced diet with enough protein and calcium, and follow NHS advice on vitamin D.

Act early on symptoms

For inflammatory arthritis, you cannot always stop it starting, but early treatment can prevent long-term joint damage. See your GP if you have joint swelling, stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes in the morning, or pain in several joints.

If you already have arthritis

The same steps also help manage existing arthritis. Exercise and weight loss are core treatments for osteoarthritis in NICE guidance. Staying active and not smoking help inflammatory arthritis treatment work better. It is never too late to start.

A realistic message

No one can promise that you will never get arthritis. But healthy habits reduce your risk and make a real difference to how arthritis affects you. Be wary of products sold as preventing arthritis, such as supplements; NICE does not recommend glucosamine or chondroitin for osteoarthritis.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
